assessment.whatTheyDo: Barcelona biotech spin-off from the Centre for Genomic Regulation that uses high-throughput genetics and AI to find small-molecule drugs for hard-to-drug protein targets.
concerns: Headquartered in Spain, so visa, relocation and time-zone issues make it materially harder for a US-based person to join.
Wet-lab drug discovery biotech, not software or product engineering. Engineers would mostly support the scientific platform.
Doesn't match any of the person's stated interest themes. At most it touches 'applied AI in a vertical', and the AI models are still planned rather than shipped.
Preclinical, with no shipped product or revenue. The AI models are described as something they will build.
No careers page or engineering roles found, so there is no evidence of senior or staff engineer hiring.
assessment.rationale: ALLOX is a credible science-led spin-off with a strong academic founder in Ben Lehner, but it is a biotech in Barcelona rather than a software or product company. It barely overlaps with the person's themes, and the geography penalty applies. The round size is in range, and the technical depth is real but in biology rather than software.
assessment.summary: ALLOX is a CRG Barcelona spin-off. It maps allosteric and regulatory sites on proteins using massively parallel mutational genetics, and it plans to add AI models. It raised a $10.5M seed led by Asabys. It is a legitimate operating company, but it is a poor fit for a US-based software engineer or PM looking for a product role.
assessment.product: A drug discovery platform that measures the effects of thousands of genetic mutations in parallel to map protein regions that affect folding and interactions. It uses this to identify allosteric and orthosteric binding sites for small-molecule drugs against hard-to-drug targets such as protein-protein interactions and transcription factors. The company plans to build proprietary AI models on this data and has internal drug programmes.
assessment.team: Co-founders are Ben Lehner, Júlia Domingo (CEO), Pablo Baeza and Andre Faure, as reported by press on the company's launch. Morten Graugaard was appointed Independent Chair of the Board. Lab and office are at CRG/PRBB in Barcelona. I did not verify team backgrounds beyond these names.
assessment.funding: An initial financing (reported as pre-seed) from Asabys' Sabadell Asabys II fund at launch. Now a $10.5M seed led by Asabys through Sabadell Asabys II, with CDTI (via SICC Innvierte) and the Institut Català de Finances (ICF) participating, per tech.eu.

Pre-clinical biotech with no shipped product
AI component still planned
No visible engineering hiring
greenFlags: Credible academic founders from the CRG
Round size in the preferred range
Proprietary experimental data platform that is more than a GPT wrapper
Specialist lead investor that remains on the board

name: Fractile
evidence: Headline: Exclusive: Fractile raises £540m in new Series C funding, filings show

assessment.whatTheyDo: Fractile is a London-based AI chip startup building in-memory-compute processors to speed up and cut the cost of LLM inference.
matchedInterests: Databases, distributed systems, and cloud infrastructure
concerns: Headquartered in the UK. Most engineering is in London and Bristol, so a US-based person would need a visa or relocation. Fractile also lists San Francisco and Taipei, but I couldn't confirm how many roles are there.

A very large round (reported £540m or about $540–600m) for a company whose chips don't appear to be in volume production. That is the 'large raise with no shipped product' pattern the person is wary of.
The team is no longer tiny. The company is scaling quickly, with a £100m expansion and a new Bristol hardware facility, so an individual engineer's leverage may be lower than at a small startup.
The work is mostly silicon, hardware and low-level ML kernels. That only partly overlaps with the person's full-stack and product background, and the product-manager angle is limited.

The Series C funding amount and stage labels are inconsistent across sources. The Sifted headline says £540m. Other press says about $600M at a $6.5B valuation. Some outlets call the May 2026 $220M round a Series B and others a Series C. I did not find confirmation that the round has closed.
Performance claims (50–100x faster, 10x cheaper) are company claims and have not been independently verified.
assessment.rationale: Fractile is a real, well-funded, technically deep AI-infrastructure company with credible backers and reported Anthropic demand, and it is hiring engineers. The score is held to the 50s because it is UK-based, the work is hardware-heavy, and the raise is very large for a company at this stage of commercialisation.
assessment.summary: Fractile is a London AI inference chip startup founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin, a PhD in AI. It uses in-memory compute to remove the memory bottleneck in running frontier models. It raised a $15M seed in 2024 and a $220M round in May 2026 led by Founders Fund and Accel. Press now reports a Series C of up to about $600M at around $6.5B, tied to a reported Anthropic chip deal. It is technically serious and well funded, but it is a non-US hardware company that is growing fast.
assessment.product: AI inference accelerators built on in-memory compute, aimed at running frontier LLMs far faster and cheaper than GPUs. Customers would be AI labs and datacenter operators. Anthropic has reportedly been in talks to buy its chips.
assessment.team: Founder and CEO Walter Goodwin has an AI PhD (Oxford robotics background per press; not verified). Pat Gelsinger, the former Intel CEO, is a reported investor. The company hires in London, Bristol, San Francisco and Taipei and is building a hardware engineering facility in Bristol.
assessment.funding: $15M seed in July 2024. A $220M round in May 2026 led by Founders Fund, Accel and Factorial Funds (labelled Series B by most outlets). A Series C reported by Sifted as £540m, with other press citing about $600M at a $6.5B pre-money valuation. Pat Gelsinger is a reported investor.
